sections.b: 1 Chronicles 21:1 is the only verse in the historical books where satan may be a heavenly figure: "Satan stood up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel." The parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD stirred David up in anger. The word has no article here, unlike "the satan" of Job and Zechariah. Readers take it as (1) the heavenly Satan, acting within God's permission, so that both books are true; (2) a human adversary, such as an enemy army whose threat moved David to count his troops (Sailhamer); (3) a heavenly attacker, perhaps the destroying angel of 21:15–16, like the angel who stood against Balaam "as an adversary" (Numbers 22:22; Day, Stokes); or (4) a later writer's unwillingness to say God moved David to sin. The Chronicler keeps David's full responsibility: "It is I who sinned" (21:17).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:1; 1 Chronicles 21:15–17; 2 Samuel 24:1; Numbers 22:22; Job 1:6–12; 1 Kings 22:19–23

common: Satan in 1 Chronicles 21:1 is usually taken as the devil, acting with God's permission, so that it agrees with 2 Samuel 24:1.
uncommon: John Sailhamer read the satan of 1 Chronicles 21:1 as a human military enemy.
Ryan Stokes argued that the satan of 1 Chronicles 21:1 is a heavenly attacker like the destroying angel later in the chapter.

sections.b: Chronicles retells David's census (21:1–6) with its own numbers, 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah, and adds that Levi and Benjamin were not counted, because Joab found the order abhorrent. Joab also asks why the count should "become guilt for Israel" (21:3). Later, in the army lists, the writer adds that David did not count those under twenty, "because the LORD had said he would make Israel as many as the stars in the sky," and that Joab's count was never finished and brought wrath (27:23–24). The twelve army divisions of 24,000 (27:1–15), totaling 288,000, raise the same question of large numbers; some read 'elef as a unit. In contrast, the counts of Levites, priests and singers in chapters 23–26 bring no judgment: they are counts for service, ordered by lot.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:1–6; 1 Chronicles 27:1–15; 1 Chronicles 27:23–24; 1 Chronicles 23:3; 2 Samuel 24:1–9; Genesis 15:5

sections.b: Chronicles calls the landowner Ornan and adds that he was threshing wheat when he saw the angel, and hid with his four sons (21:20). David asks for the floor "for its full price in silver," Abraham's phrase for the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:9), and pays six hundred shekels of gold for "the place" (21:22–25). God answers with fire from heaven, the angel sheathes his sword, and David declares, "This is the house of the LORD God" (22:1). 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies the site as Mount Moriah.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:15–22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Genesis 23:9; Judges 6:11

sections.b: Only Chronicles names the temple's hill: Solomon's house "stood on Mount Moriah... at the place David had made ready: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite" (2 Chronicles 3:1), the place David chose after the plague (1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1). Moriah is the land where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2), and Jewish tradition joined the two sites. The Talmud reads "the LORD saw" in 1 Chronicles 21:15 as God seeing the ashes of Isaac (Bavli Berakhot 62b), linking it with Abraham's name for the place, "The LORD Will See" (Genesis 22:14). Many critical scholars think the identification of Moriah with Jerusalem is the Chronicler's or his tradition's, since Genesis does not make it; Samaritans locate Moriah at Mount Gerizim.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:15; 1 Chronicles 22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 22:14

sections.b: In Kings, Solomon plans and builds the temple. In 1 Chronicles 22–29, David does almost everything but build it: he names the site (22:1), gathers stone, iron, bronze and cedar and vast sums of gold and silver (22:2–5, 22:14; 29:2–5), organizes the Levites, priests, singers, gatekeepers and treasurers (23–26), and hands Solomon a written pattern "from the LORD's hand" (28:11–19), as Moses received the pattern of the tabernacle (Exodus 25:9, 25:40). The reason he cannot build is that he has shed much blood (22:8; 28:3), and the builder must be a man of rest (22:9). The leaders and people give freely for the work (29:6–9). Traditional readers take this as history Kings did not tell; critical scholars see the Chronicler giving the temple of his own day David's authority.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 22:1–19; 1 Chronicles 28:2–21; 1 Chronicles 29:1–9; 1 Kings 5–7; Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40

claude.title: Claude's theory: a temple founded on a stopped judgment
claude.body: This is my own reading. In Chronicles the temple's site is not chosen for its height, beauty or history but because God's judgment stopped there (21:15) and fire answered a king's confession (21:26). The temple's first meaning is therefore mercy after sin, which Solomon's prayer develops (2 Chronicles 6:24–39; 7:14). The link of site and mercy is often noted for 2 Samuel 24, which P. Kyle McCarter reads as the founding story of the altar on the temple site; I am suggesting that Chronicles, by tying 22:1 directly to 21:30, makes it the founding idea of the whole temple section.

sections.b: In 1 Chronicles 21 the LORD's angel is a destroyer. He brings plague through Israel's territory (21:12), is sent to ruin Jerusalem (21:15), stands "between earth and sky, his sword drawn in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem" (21:16), gives the prophet Gad his message (21:18), and sheathes his sword at God's word (21:27). The image recalls the angel with a drawn sword before Balaam (Numbers 22:23) and before Joshua (Joshua 5:13). The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a seems to have had the same scene in its text of 2 Samuel 24.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:12–30; 2 Samuel 24:16; Numbers 22:23; Joshua 5:13; 2 Kings 19:35

sections.h: Priests and Levites in David's plan
sections.b: 1 Chronicles 23–26 is the Bible's fullest picture of the temple staff. The Levites, thirty-eight thousand strong, are assigned as overseers, officials and judges, gatekeepers and musicians (23:3–5). With the tabernacle at rest they no longer carry it (23:26); they help Aaron's sons, keep the courts and rooms, bake the bread and grain offerings, and sing praise morning and evening (23:28–31). Only Aaron's descendants handle the most holy things (23:13). The priests are divided into twenty-four courses by lot (24:1–19), and Levite families into watches. The starting age shifts from thirty (23:3) to twenty (23:24, 23:27). Many scholars think these chapters argue for the Levites' standing in the second temple.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 23:1–32; 1 Chronicles 24:1–31; 1 Chronicles 26:1–32; Numbers 3–4; Numbers 8:24–26; Ezra 3:8

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 24 tells how the courses were made. Sixteen heads of families came from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar, since Nadab and Abihu died without sons (24:1–4). Their order was drawn by lot before David, Zadok, Ahimelech and the heads of families, and a Levite scribe, Shemaiah, wrote it down (24:5–6). The list (24:7–18) begins with Jehoiarib, the course of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:1), and puts Abijah eighth (24:10), the course of Zechariah in Luke 1:5. The courses "came into the LORD's house" by the rule Aaron gave them (24:19). The other Levites (24:20–31), the singers (25:9–31) and the gatekeepers (26:12–19) are ordered by the same lot. Many scholars, such as H. G. M. Williamson, think the full system of twenty-four took shape after the exile and was credited to David; traditional readers take it as David's own work.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 24:1–19; 1 Chronicles 24:20–31; 1 Chronicles 25:9–31; 1 Chronicles 26:12–19; 1 Maccabees 2:1; Luke 1:5

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 25 completes the singers' story. David and the army commanders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun "who prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals" (25:1): four sons of Asaph, six of Jeduthun, and fourteen sons and three daughters of Heman, "the king's visionary" (25:5). The names of Heman's last nine sons may form a line of a psalm (25:4). Each group served "under their father's hand," and the fathers "at the king's direction" (25:6). The 288 trained singers were then divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, "the small the same as the great, the master the same as the pupil" (25:7–8), on the pattern of the priestly courses of chapter 24. Readers take the singers' prophesying as inspired song, as Spirit-led praise, or as a claim by the singers of the Chronicler's day to a prophet's authority.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 25:1–31; 1 Chronicles 24:7–18; 2 Chronicles 20:14; 2 Chronicles 35:15

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 23:5 sets four thousand Levites to praise the LORD "on the instruments I have made for praising him," which makes David a maker of instruments as well as a singer (compare 2 Chronicles 7:6; 2 Chronicles 29:26–27; Amos 6:5). The singers of chapter 25 play lyres, harps and cymbals (25:1, 25:6). Their families, their lots and their place in the Psalms are treated on the topic on Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 23:5; 1 Chronicles 25:1; 1 Chronicles 25:6; 2 Chronicles 7:6; 2 Chronicles 29:26–27; Amos 6:5

sections.b: In 1 Chronicles 25:1–5 the temple singers "prophesied" with lyres, harps and cymbals, Jeduthun "prophesied with the lyre, giving thanks and praise," and Heman was "the king's visionary." The link between music and prophecy appears in Samuel's band of prophets (1 Samuel 10:5) and in Elisha's call for a musician (2 Kings 3:15). Readers see inspired song, a broadening of the word to cover Spirit-led praise, or a claim by the singers of the Chronicler's day to the authority of prophets. In 2 Chronicles 20:14 a Levite of Asaph's family prophesies in the assembly.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 25:1–5; 1 Samuel 10:5; 2 Kings 3:15; 2 Chronicles 20:14; 2 Chronicles 35:15

sections.b: David's last prayer (1 Chronicles 29:10–19) blesses God "from the ages past to the ages to come," confesses that "Yours, LORD, is the kingdom," and admits that all Israel can give comes from God's hand, since "we are foreigners before you, and lodgers, as all our fathers were." It ends by asking God to keep the people's hearts steady and to give Solomon a whole heart. Jews recite 29:10–13 every morning. Christians know 29:11 through the doxology that later manuscripts add to the Lord's Prayer at Matthew 6:13, which the KJV renders "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory." It is first found in a shorter form in the Didache. Most scholars think the doxology was added there; defenders of the Byzantine text, such as Maurice Robinson, hold it original.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 29:10–19; Matthew 6:13; Psalm 39:12; Leviticus 25:23

sections.b: In 1 Chronicles 22:9–10 and 28:5–7 David tells Solomon and the leaders what God promised: a son, a man of rest, who will build God's house, "He will be a son to me, and I will be a father to him" (22:10), and whose kingdom God will make secure for all time. Chronicles names Solomon as the son and calls the throne "the throne of the LORD's kingdom" (28:5; 29:23). It adds a condition: "if he holds firm in doing my commands and my rulings" (28:7; compare 28:9). Readers relate the condition to the unconditional promise of 2 Samuel 7:14–16 in different ways: kings can fall but the line endures, the promise is fulfilled in the Messiah, or later writers added the condition after the exile.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 22:9–10; 1 Chronicles 28:4–7; 1 Chronicles 29:23; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11–12; Hebrews 1:5

sections.b: Chronicles introduces Solomon as the son God named before his birth, "a man of rest" whose name echoes shalom (22:9). He is "young and tender" (22:5; 29:1), receives the plans and materials from David (28:11–21), and is made king twice, once in summary (23:1) and once before the assembly with Zadok anointed as priest (29:22). Unlike 1 Kings 1–2, there is no rival: all David's sons pledge loyalty (29:24). Solomon sits "on the LORD's throne" and receives royal splendor beyond any king before him (29:23–25).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 22:5–19; 1 Chronicles 23:1; 1 Chronicles 28:5–10; 1 Chronicles 29:1; 1 Chronicles 29:22–25; 1 Kings 1:1–53

sections.b: Chronicles ends David's story with preparation, not decline. After the census and plague (1 Chronicles 21), David chooses the temple site, gathers materials, organizes the Levites, priests, singers, gatekeepers, army and stewards (22–27), and in public assemblies hands Solomon the plan and the charge (28–29). He gives his own treasure and leads the people in prayer (29:3, 29:10–19). There is no bedridden king, no Adonijah, no deathbed orders about Joab and Shimei as in 1 Kings 1–2. David dies "at a good old age, satisfied with days, riches and glory" (29:28), the words used of Abraham.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21–29; 1 Kings 1:1–2:12; Genesis 25:8

sections.b: Chronicles makes Zadok David's partner in dividing the priests (24:3, 24:6, 24:31), traces him to Eleazar, and pairs him with Ahimelech son of Abiathar from Ithamar's line, repeating the name order of 2 Samuel 8:17. At Solomon's second coronation "they anointed him for the LORD as ruler, and Zadok as priest" (29:22), the only mention of Zadok's anointing. A Zadok also leads the Aaronites in the tribal list (27:17).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 24:3–6; 1 Chronicles 24:31; 1 Chronicles 27:17; 1 Chronicles 29:22; 2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Kings 2:35

sections.b: Chronicles speaks of Israel's throne as God's own: Solomon will "sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom over Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:5), and he "sat on the LORD's throne as king" (29:23). David's prayer declares, "Yours, LORD, is the kingdom" (29:11). The king is God's steward. The chapters also show the practical side of kingship: a rotating militia (27:1–15), tribal leaders (27:16–22), stewards over royal lands and herds (27:25–31) and counselors (27:32–34).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 28:5; 1 Chronicles 29:11; 1 Chronicles 29:23; 1 Chronicles 17:14; 1 Chronicles 27:1–34; 2 Chronicles 9:8

sections.b: In 1 Chronicles 24–26 every rota is fixed by lot: the twenty-four priestly courses (24:5–19), the Levite families (24:31), the twenty-four groups of singers, "the small the same as the great, the master the same as the pupil" (25:8), and the gatekeepers' posts (26:13–16). The lot keeps any family from claiming the best turns and leaves the order to God. Luke shows the same practice in the first century: Zechariah was chosen by lot to burn incense (Luke 1:9).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 24:5; 1 Chronicles 24:31; 1 Chronicles 25:8; 1 Chronicles 26:13; Luke 1:9; Proverbs 16:33

sections.b: Chronicles carefully links the temple to Moses' tabernacle. The tabernacle and its altar stood at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 21:29), but God's fire on David's new altar made the threshing floor the place of sacrifice (21:26–22:1). With the ark at rest, the Levites no longer carry the tabernacle (23:26). David receives a "pattern" as Moses did (28:11–19; Exodus 25:9, 25:40), and the leaders give freely, as the people did for the tabernacle (29:6–9; Exodus 35:21–29).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:29; 1 Chronicles 23:26; 1 Chronicles 28:11–19; 1 Chronicles 29:6–9; Exodus 25:9; Exodus 35:21–29

sections.b: These chapters describe worship as organized and joyful. Levites stand every morning and evening to give thanks and praise (23:30), singers prophesy with instruments (25:1), and offerings follow the calendar of Sabbaths, New Moons and feasts (23:31). At the end the people give freely "with a whole heart" (29:9), David blesses God before the assembly (29:10–19), the assembly bows before the LORD and the king (29:20), and they offer sacrifices and eat and drink with great joy before the LORD (29:21–22). David's words "What we have given you came out of your own hand" (29:14) are used at the offering in many churches.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 23:30–31; 1 Chronicles 25:1; 1 Chronicles 29:9–22

sections.b: The twelve commanders of David's monthly divisions in 1 Chronicles 27:2–15 are almost all names from the list of mighty men (11:10–47; 2 Samuel 23:8–39): Jashobeam, Dodai (the father of Eleazar), Benaiah, Asahel, Shamhuth, Ira, Helez, Sibbecai, Abiezer, Maharai, Benaiah of Pirathon and Heldai. Asahel had died early in David's reign (2 Samuel 2:23), so the list adds his son Zebadiah (27:7).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 27:2–15; 1 Chronicles 11:10–47; 2 Samuel 23:8–39; 2 Samuel 2:18–23

sections.b: Chronicles builds its temple theology on rest. God promised David a son who would be "a man of rest," to whom God would give rest from his enemies and peace and calm in Israel (1 Chronicles 22:9). God has given rest on all sides (22:18) and settled in Jerusalem (23:25), so the Levites no longer carry the tabernacle (23:26). The temple is "a resting house for the ark" (28:2), as Psalm 132:8 and 2 Chronicles 6:41 sing. This fulfills Deuteronomy 12:9–11, where rest from enemies comes before the chosen place.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 22:9; 1 Chronicles 22:18; 1 Chronicles 23:25–26; 1 Chronicles 28:2; Deuteronomy 12:9–11; Psalm 132:8

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 21:29–30 explains why David did not sacrifice at Gibeon after the plague: "At that time the LORD's tabernacle, the one Moses made in the wilderness, stood at the high place in Gibeon, with the altar of burnt offering," but David was terrified of the angel's sword. So the altar on Ornan's threshing floor, answered by fire from heaven, became the legitimate place of sacrifice, and Gibeon's role ends with Solomon's visit (2 Chronicles 1:3–6).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 21:29–30; 1 Chronicles 16:39–40; 2 Chronicles 1:3–6; 1 Kings 3:4
